title: Introduction to Programming
summary: Your first programming course: Java from primitive types and loops to classes, inheritance, equals and hashCode, exceptions, file I/O, unit tests, streams and threads, all in one quarter. Each week has three lectures that mix theory with live coding, plus lab sessions with eight practice assignments. The grade comes from two exams of equal weight: a closed-book theory exam on WebLab and a three-hour programming exam in IntelliJ.

basis.description: Slides of Lectures 1 to 20 of CSE1100 (2024-25) as text, the WebLab exercises and lab assignments, and the 2023 to 2025 theory and programming papers. Time shares count content slides; Lecture 0 (course organisation) and Lecture 21 (exam practice) are left out.
basis.caveat: The material is from CSE1100, the old code; from 2026-27 the course is CSE11B, with content unchanged, and you need it to enter CSE200 Software Project. Older papers carry the former name Object Oriented Programming. Lectures 9 and 10 share one slide deck, and the I/O decks step through long code examples slide by slide, so I/O looks bigger in slides than in lecture time.

topics.name: Java basics: types, operators and control flow
know: The [[eight primitive types, their ranges]], two's complement storage, and how int and double arithmetic differ (integer division, modulo, overflow)
Implicit widening versus explicit casts, and what a cast to int does to a double
Equality, relational, boolean [[logical (& and |) versus conditional (&& and ||)]] operators, short-circuit evaluation and bitwise operators on integers
if/else, [[switch with and without break (fall-through)]], for, while and do-while, and when each loop fits
What == compares for primitives and for references
do: Trace a loop or switch by hand and state the exact output
Evaluate an expression mixing bitwise, boolean and arithmetic operators
Write nested loops that build a text pattern of stars and other characters into a String
pitfalls: Forgetting that a switch without break falls through into the next case
Expecting 7 / 2 to give 3.5, or & to short-circuit like &&

topics.name: Methods, arrays and recursion
know: Method signature, parameters, return type and void methods, and the lifetime of local variables
[[Java is always pass by value]]: for an object or array [[the reference is copied, not the object]]
Arrays: creation, fixed length, default values, traversal, and copying an array versus copying the reference
Standard array patterns: reduction (sum, max), filtering, linear search
Recursion with a base case, and why deep recursion ends in a [[StackOverflowError]]
do: Predict what a swap method does to primitives versus to array elements
Implement a class around a String or int array that adds, removes, shifts or rotates elements
Read a recursive method and say for which inputs it terminates or overflows the stack
pitfalls: Believing a method can swap two int arguments in the caller
Off-by-one errors and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at the array edges

topics.name: Classes, composition and collections
know: Class versus object, fields, constructors, this, static versus instance members, and encapsulation with private fields and getters
[[Stack and heap: where variables, objects and Strings live]], and how many objects exist after a piece of code runs
null and the NullPointerException; [[final fields cannot be reassigned]], so a setter on them does not compile
Writing a container class on top of an array, then ArrayList and Set from the library, and how ArrayList grows internally
Composition (a class holding objects of other classes) versus inheritance, and [[composition over inheritance]] when a property is not a kind of the class
Packages, import, and reading the Javadoc of library classes
do: Draw the stack and heap for a short program and count the objects created
Choose between a String attribute, a composed class or a subclass for a described design
Turn a problem text into model classes and a container class, as the Program Design lecture does for an animal shelter
Implement list operations with ArrayList: add, remove, contains, copy, filter
pitfalls: Storing everything in Strings or in one big main class: the programming rubric gives no design points for that
Confusing a shallow copy (clone of an ArrayList) with copies of the elements

topics.name: Testing, debugging and code quality
know: JUnit 5: [[@Test, assertEquals, assertTrue, assertNotSame, assertThrows]], and the difference between assertEquals and assertSame
Unit versus integration tests, positive versus negative tests, and line coverage as a measure of enough testing
The debugger: breakpoints, conditional and hit-count breakpoints, watchpoints, stepping and inspecting values
Quality rules: short methods, no duplicated code (pull shared code into an abstract parent), low cyclomatic complexity, short parameter lists, naming conventions
Javadoc comments with a description and [[@param and @return]], and Checkstyle as the tool that checks style
do: Write a test class that reaches 80 percent line coverage with one test per non-trivial method
Decide whether a given test passes, fails or does not compile
Test code that reads input by giving a Scanner a String instead of a file
pitfalls: Thinking high cyclomatic complexity is a sign of good internal quality: [[lower is better]]
Leaving @param fields empty in Javadoc, which the programming exam marks down

topics.name: Inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces
know: extends, super() and the order of construction, default constructors, and the access levels private, package, protected and public
The Liskov Substitution Principle: [[a subclass object may stand wherever its superclass is expected]], not the other way round
[[Declared (static) versus actual (dynamic) type]], and which casts the compiler accepts
Overloading versus overriding; [[static binding by the compiler versus dynamic binding by the JVM]]
Abstract classes, interfaces, default methods, and final to stop overriding
do: Given a class hierarchy and a main method, say which lines compile and what each call prints
Explain static and dynamic binding in your own words with an example where they differ
Design an inheritance hierarchy with an abstract parent for the item types in an exam scenario
pitfalls: Defining binding as working out the type of a variable: the midterm feedback names this as the most common mistake
Claiming static binding only applies to static, private or final methods
Calling a subclass-only method through a superclass reference and expecting it to compile

topics.name: Equality and hashCode
know: == versus equals, and the default equals in Object
The equals contract: [[reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, false for null]]
Why [[getClass() is preferred over instanceof]] once subclasses are involved
hashCode: [[equal objects must have equal hash codes]]; buckets, compression and collisions in a HashSet or HashMap
Objects.equals and Objects.hash, and the equals and hashCode that a record generates
do: Write equals and hashCode for a class with String, int and List fields, including null fields and order-independent comparison
Predict the result of equals, assertEquals or a HashSet lookup on two separately created objects
pitfalls: Comparing String fields with == inside equals
Calling o.getClass() before checking o for null
Overriding equals but not hashCode, which breaks HashSet and HashMap

topics.name: Exceptions
know: Errors versus exceptions, and [[checked versus unchecked (RuntimeException)]] exceptions
try, catch and finally, and that [[catch blocks must go from specific to general]]
Propagation along the call stack and the default exception handler
The throws clause versus throwing with throw, and writing your own exception class
do: Decide from the Javadoc whether an exception is checked and what the compiler then demands
Say which catch block runs, and whether two orderings of catch blocks compile
pitfalls: Saying a checked exception must be both caught and declared: [[either one is enough]]
Thinking a throws clause stops the exception from reaching the default handler: it only passes it on

topics.name: Strings, file input and output
know: String methods (split, substring, trim, indexOf, toUpperCase) and Character helpers, plus String immutability
Scanner on System.in, a file or a String: [[next, nextInt, nextLine, hasNext and useDelimiter]]
java.io: [[Reader and Writer for characters, InputStream and OutputStream for bytes]], buffering with BufferedReader, and PrintWriter for output
Closing resources, and handling FileNotFoundException and IOException
Object streams and Serializable for saving whole objects
do: Parse a semi-structured text file whose records span several lines into objects, without hardcoding the file name
Build a looping text menu that reads choices from System.in and handles wrong input
Write a list of objects to a Writer in an exact output format
Transform strings, for example to camelCase, using String and Character methods
pitfalls: Mixing nextInt and nextLine on one Scanner and losing a line
A reader that only works for the exact order of the example file: the rubric tests it with other input files

topics.name: Generics, functional and modern Java
know: Generic classes such as Box<T>, raw types, autoboxing of int to Integer, type erasure and bounded types
Lambdas and functional interfaces (Predicate, Function), and the imperative versus functional paradigm
Stream pipelines: a source, intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct) and [[one terminal operation]] (collect, count, max, average); [[a stream is used once]]
Optional and the primitive versions such as OptionalInt, returned by max or findFirst on a possibly empty stream
var, enums, switch expressions, sealed classes, records, and [[Comparable versus Comparator]] for sorting
do: Solve a task with streams and Optional only, without loops, recursion or collections
Say the type and value a stream expression produces on empty input
Write a record and know which class it is equivalent to
Use replaceAll with a lambda or a Comparator on a List in the programming exam
pitfalls: Returning null where an Optional is expected, or assuming max of an empty IntStream gives a number
Falling back on a loop in a question that demands a functional solution: that exercise then scores 0

topics.name: Threads
know: Threads versus processes, concurrency versus parallelism, interleaving on one core and hyperthreading
Starting a thread: a subclass of Thread or a Runnable, [[start versus run]], and Thread.ofPlatform
[[The OS scheduler decides the order]], so output order is not fixed
synchronized methods and blocks, race conditions, and deadlock
do: List which output orders are possible for two threads calling a synchronized method
Move one calculation of a menu option into a separate thread, as Programming Endterm 2025 asked
pitfalls: Calling run instead of start, which [[runs the code in the current thread]]
Assuming threads run in the order they were started

prerequisites: None officially: the course starts from zero
The faculty advises an online Java tutorial before the quarter, and an entry test on WebLab shows where you stand
practical: Eight lab assignments, about one per teaching week, take 4 to 6 hours each. The first ones run on WebLab, the later ones in IntelliJ, and they grow towards exam-sized programs that read a file, model it in classes and offer a menu. They are not graded, but TAs give feedback in the labs. Short weekly WebLab exercises (multiple choice plus small coding tasks) come with each lecture. The week 5 midterm and the week 8 mock programming exam do not count directly but earn bonus points.
studyAdvice: Keep up from day one: the course moves from loops to inheritance in four weeks, and the midterm in week 5 covers all of it.
Do every lab assignment yourself in IntelliJ before its deadline; the programming exam is the same kind of task under a three-hour limit.
Spend the most time on classes and composition, inheritance, file reading and testing: together they carry about three fifths of the exam points.
Practise tracing code without an IDE, because the theory exam gives you only WebLab and the Java documentation.
Learn to write equals and hashCode from memory with getClass(); every analysed paper rewards them.
Sit the mock programming exam and queue for feedback afterwards: it earns bonus and shows where your time goes.
For open questions, practise short precise definitions with an example: wrong extra claims cost points even next to correct ones.
